newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Raurimu killings ignites New Zealand gun debate.
newsitem.headline: Raurimu killings ignites New Zealand gun debate.

text.p: A fierce debate over New Zealand's liberal gun laws has been reignited by the shotgun slayings of six people in a rural central North Island town.

The gunman, wielding a 12-gauge shotgun, killed six people and seriously wounded five others in the rampage through Raurimu on Saturday. A 22-year-old man has been charged with at least one of the murders and more charges may follow.
Gun policy researcher Philip Alpers and the opposition Labour Party immediately said the killings reinforced the need for tighter gun laws.
Alpers said New Zealand lagged behind Australia, Britain and Canada in tightening ownership controls.
"Australia, Canada and Britain -- and most of the developed world -- have left us far behind. What are we waiting for?" he said in a statement.
Police Minister Jack Elder agreed the problem had gone "out of control" but appealed for a calm, measured assessment.
"We've had the problem for a long time and we have let it get out of control," Elder said in a television interview, saying guns had been getting into the wrong hands.
"We have to get it under control and cannot continue like this or we will start to look like Los Angeles," he told the weekly national paper, Sunday News.
Elder pointed to an independent review of the legislation by former High Court judge Thomas Thorp, which will not be complete until June.
"I want to see it (a review) done as quickly as possible like everyone else but I'd prefer to get it right than rush into something and not get it right," he said.
New Zealanders own a gun for every household, or 11 times as many guns per capita as the British and 60 percent more than the Australians, Alpers said.
The tradition of high gun ownership was due partly to farmers and others living in the country keeping guns for pest control and game shooting.

The gun lobby immediately hit back at the calls for tighter controls. Coalition New Zealand Licensed Firearm Users spokesman Gordon Clark said it was frustrating to hear such comments every time someone ran amok.
He believed the government should be looking more at improving the mental health system than changing the gun laws.
"When people go berserk with guns you more often than not find some sort of psychiatric problem," he said.

Labour women's affairs spokeswoman Dianne Yates said Saturday's killings and the shooting of a bank officer in Naenae, near Wellington, on January 29 reinforced the need for prompt changes to New Zealand's "inadequate" gun laws.
She said the government should not wait until June to complete its review.

In six out of ten gun controls adopted by Australia, Canada and Britain, New Zealand stood alone in not having a ban on military-style semi-automatic weapons, only requiring relicensing inspections of gun owners every 10 years and not registering guns individually.
"Our current laws allow anyone with a shooter's licence to buy and keep any number of rifles and shotguns in any home without any official record of the guns being kept anywhere," Alpers said.
"Apparently it was one of these guns -- a harmless' sporting long gun -- which was used at Raurimu," he said.

Alpers said it took less than two weeks for Britain and Australia to announce an overhaul of their gun laws after the Dunblane killings of 16 children and their teacher and the slaughter of 35 people in Tasmania last year.
"What will it take New Zealand?" he said.
